content: 1. A study by Blouin et al. (2011) evaluated the impact of a two-component intervention aimed at changing hospital practices from early to delayed umbilical cord clamping in the Peruvian Amazon. The findings were published in the Revista Panamericana de Salud Pública. 2. Another study by Blouin et al. (2013) investigated the timing of umbilical cord clamping and its relationship with infant anemia, particularly considering the role of maternal anemia. This research was published in Paediatrics International Child Health. 3. The World Health Organization (WHO) has issued guidelines recommending delayed umbilical cord clamping to improve maternal and infant health and nutritional outcomes. These guidelines are accessible through the WHO's official website. 4. Ethical considerations in medical practice are discussed in foundational texts such as What is Ethics? by Andre and Velasquez (1987) and Principles of Biomedical Ethics by Beauchamp and Childress (6th edition, 2008). 5. The WHO Regional Office for Europe published a declaration in 1994 promoting patients' rights in Europe, emphasizing the importance of ethical healthcare delivery. 6. The United Nations General Assembly adopted the Convention on the Rights of the Child, which underscores the protection and promotion of children's health and well-being. 7. Gillon (1994) proposed a framework for medical ethics based on four principles, with an emphasis on the scope of their application, as published in the BMJ. 8. Braveman and Gruskin (2003) defined health equity in the context of social justice, highlighting its importance in public health, as detailed in the Journal of Epidemiology and Community Health. 9. Schreck et al. (2010) explored how human rights can advance health equity in the global marketplace, as published in Social Science & Medicine. 10. Braveman et al. (2011) discussed health disparities and health equity as issues of justice in the American Journal of Public Health. 11. The American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) issued Committee Opinion No. 399 in February 2008, addressing umbilical cord blood banking practices, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology. 12. Rucinski et al. (2010) examined the opinions and beliefs about cord blood donation among Hispanic and non-Hispanic Black women, as published in Transfusion. 13. Samuel and Kerridge (2007) discussed emerging ethical issues related to umbilical cord blood banking in Australia, as detailed in the Journal of Bioethical Inquiry. 14. WHO expert advisory panels and committees provide guidance on various health topics, including maternal and child health, nutrition, and infectious diseases. 15. Mathai et al. (2014) summarized WHO recommendations for the prevention of postpartum hemorrhage, accessible through the WHO's website. 16. The Cochrane Collaboration provides systematic reviews of interventions, with resources available through their official website. 17. Guyatt et al. (2011) introduced the GRADE guidelines, which provide evidence profiles and summaries of findings for clinical recommendations, as published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 18. WHO guidelines for managing postpartum hemorrhage and retained placenta are available online, offering evidence-based recommendations for healthcare providers. 19. Ongoing clinical trials, such as the PREMOD trial and the Australian Placental Transfusion Study, are investigating the effects of delayed cord clamping and cord milking in preterm and term infants. 20. The WHO Steering Committee for Nutrition Guidelines Development includes experts in maternal, newborn, and child health, as well as nutrition and public health. 21. The WHO Secretariat and external resource experts contribute to the development of guidelines, ensuring a multidisciplinary approach to global health challenges. 22. WHO regional offices and external experts, such as those from UNICEF, the World Food Programme, and academic institutions, collaborate to address health and nutrition issues worldwide. 23. The WHO guideline on delayed umbilical cord clamping includes annexes detailing ongoing trials, expert contributions, and regional office activities to support its implementation. This transformation provides a clear and professional summary of the references and acknowledgments, maintaining the specificity and context of the original content.
